newsitem.title: USA: Insurers object to U.S. bank reform provisions.
newsitem.headline: Insurers object to U.S. bank reform provisions.

text.p: Six property-and-casualty insurance trade groups said Thursday they have substantial objections to portions of the Clinton administration's bank reform plan dealing with their industry.
The House Banking Committee is currently drafting legislation, based in part on the Clinton plan, to overhaul U.S. financial laws and allow banks to sell insurance.

"We think it is critical that our concerns are addressed as the committee moves forward in its effort to develop a balanced piece of financial reform legislation," the groups said in a letter to committee chairman Jim Leach.
The Iowa Republican said earlier this week he hoped to draft a new bank reform bill incorporating much of Clinton's plan by Friday and begin a mark up next week.

Under the Clinton plan, federal bank regulators could in some cases overrule state insurance regulations that applied to national banks. The insurance trade groups said the provision was too broad and lacked a neutral forum for resolving conflicts between federal and state authorities.
"These principles deal with the fundamental fairness of any new financial modernization regime and are a necessary predicate to positive action on legislation," the groups said.

Federal preemption of state insurance regulation is considered one of the most significant unresolved issues preventing Congress from reforming antiquated banking laws based on the 1933 Glass-Steagall Act.
In their letter, the insurance groups also staked out a position favoring the mixing of banking and commerce, another burning controversy in the current debate.
"Insurers have long held commercial investments that are permitted and regulated by state insurance holding company laws," the groups said.
"Without the ability to make and hold such investments, insurer acquisition of banks would be impractical," the groups added.
Under current law, bank holding companies may not own commercial enterprises, although a commercial company may own a single savings and loan institution.
Lawmakers have offered several proposals on the subject, and the the Clinton plan offered two new alternatives without endorsing either side of the argument.

Under one option, financial holding companies could conduct a limited "basket" of commercial activity but commercial companies with more than $750 million of assets could not own banks. Under a second option, the current bank prohibition would be retained but the current exception for thrifts would also continue.

Leach has been a strong opponent of mixing banking and commerce, along with some Senate Democrats, small banks, labor and consumer groups. Federal Reserve chairman Alan Greenspan last month also came out against allowing such combinations as part of bank reform legislation.

The groups that signed the letter were the Alliance of American Insurers, American Insurance Association, Council of Insurance Agents & Brokers, National Association of Independent Insurers, National Association of Mutual Insurance Companies, and Reinsurance Association of America.
